review: Timing-experiment sources reviewed 2026-10-14; earlier lessons retain their source-specific scope. Editorial review, not independent expert validation. Activity timing and intensity are authored.

allen.title: Allen Human Reference Atlas – 3D, 2020
allen.finding: An anatomical parcellation of the ICBM 2009b symmetric reference. The rendered meshes are derived from labeled voxels.
allen.limit: A symmetric reference atlas, not a scan of you. Teaching groups combine atlas labels; they are not functional parcels.

music.title: Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music
music.finding: The study reported striatal dopamine release during intensely pleasurable music, with caudate involvement during anticipation and nucleus accumbens involvement during peak responses.
music.limit: Selected listeners and stimuli. PET release inference and complementary fMRI responses do not provide a universal second-by-second dopamine concentration.

reward.title: A Neural Substrate of Prediction and Reward
reward.finding: Dopaminergic responses can reflect differences between predicted and obtained reward. Learned predictions change responses to cues and outcomes.
reward.limit: A simplified teaching account of a subset of dopaminergic responses. The human atlas localization and animation are schematic.

vision.title: Distributed and overlapping representations of faces and objects in ventral temporal cortex
vision.finding: Faces and objects elicited discriminable, distributed patterns in ventral temporal cortex. Information was not restricted to the maximally responding patch.
vision.limit: Broad atlas gyri stand in for the study’s patterns. Display intensity and stage timing are authored; they are not the original fMRI values.

motor.title: Function in the Human Connectome: Task-fMRI and Individual Differences in Behavior
motor.finding: The HCP task battery includes movement conditions to examine functional activation. A controlled task and its contrast define what an activation map means.
motor.limit: The lesson highlights broad anatomical participants; it does not replay an HCP dataset or resolve finger somatotopy.

brain.title: Physiology, Brain
brain.finding: Brain functions arise through interacting cortical, subcortical, cerebellar and brainstem systems.
brain.limit: Short region descriptions are introductory summaries, not exhaustive or exclusive functional assignments.

basal.title: Neuroanatomy, Basal Ganglia
basal.finding: Basal ganglia participate in circuits related to action, learning and cognition, through interactions with cortex and thalamus.
basal.limit: Individual pathways contain cell-type and receptor-specific effects that a regional atlas does not resolve.

synthesis.title: Neurotransmitter Synthesis
synthesis.finding: Synthesis, vesicle packaging, release and clearance are distinct processes. Small molecules and peptides have different synthesis and transport pathways.
synthesis.limit: The synapse is a representative diagram with expanded space and slowed teaching time, not a molecular recording.

receptors.title: Two Families of Postsynaptic Receptors
receptors.finding: Ionotropic receptors directly gate ion channels. Metabotropic receptors act through intracellular signaling pathways.
receptors.limit: A transmitter’s effect depends on receptor type and cellular context, not its name alone.

glutamate.title: Glutamatergic Signaling in the Central Nervous System
glutamate.finding: Glutamate signals through both ionotropic and metabotropic receptor families, with different downstream effects.
glutamate.limit: The AMPA-like teaching diagram represents one mechanism; it does not represent all glutamate receptors.

catecholamines.title: Physiology, Catecholamines
catecholamines.finding: Dopamine synthesis proceeds from tyrosine through L-DOPA. Dopamine is also a precursor in the catecholamine pathway.
catecholamines.limit: Precursor availability or an activity choice does not determine a visitor’s dopamine level.

neurotransmitters.title: Neurotransmitters
neurotransmitters.finding: Neurotransmitters act through diverse receptors; neurons can use more than one signaling molecule.
neurotransmitters.limit: Excitation and inhibition depend on receptor and cellular conditions. No single chemical corresponds to one feeling.

bold.title: Neurophysiological investigation of the basis of the fMRI signal
bold.finding: BOLD is an indirect neurovascular signal; in the studied visual cortex conditions it related more strongly to local field potentials than to multi-unit output.
bold.limit: fMRI brightness cannot be converted directly into spike counts or chemical release.

wilson.title: Excitatory and inhibitory interactions in localized populations of model neurons
wilson.finding: Coupled excitatory and inhibitory populations can produce nonlinear temporal behavior.
wilson.limit: Our simplified rate model uses pedagogical parameters, not parameters fitted to a person or a particular brain region.

yeo.title: The organization of the human cerebral cortex estimated by intrinsic functional connectivity
yeo.authors: Yeo et al. · Journal of Neurophysiology
yeo.finding: Large-scale cortical networks can be estimated from patterns of functional connectivity.
yeo.limit: Network membership does not imply a unique mental function or a directed anatomical connection.

release.title: Calcium Control of Neurotransmitter Release
release.authors: Südhof · Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology
release.finding: Calcium entry couples electrical activity to vesicular release through calcium sensing and membrane fusion machinery.
release.limit: Geometry, particle counts, diffusion paths and timing in this teaching view are authored, not molecular dynamics or measured kinetics.

neuron-morphology.title: Pyramidal neurons: dendritic structure and synaptic integration
neuron-morphology.method: Review of neuronal structure and integration
neuron-morphology.finding: Pyramidal neurons have distinct apical and basal dendritic trees; dendritic structure participates in synaptic integration.
neuron-morphology.limit: The enlarged neural tissue window is procedural teaching geometry. Cell positions, density, contacts and flashes are not reconstructed from the atlas or calibrated to recordings.

stdp-bi-poo.title: Synaptic modifications in cultured hippocampal neurons: dependence on spike timing, synaptic strength, and postsynaptic cell type
stdp-bi-poo.finding: Repeated pre/post spike pairings changed glutamatergic synaptic efficacy with timing-dependent direction; initial strength and postsynaptic cell type also mattered.
stdp-bi-poo.limit: A specific experimental preparation, not a universal rule for every synapse. doke uses an abstract imposed-spike pairing protocol and authored parameters; eight pairings are a teaching shortcut, not a reproduced biological learning rate.

stdp-model.title: Neuronal Dynamics §19.2: Models of Hebbian learning
stdp-model.finding: Pair-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity can be expressed through decaying pre/post traces, with explicit pair selection and weight bounds.
stdp-model.limit: doke uses additive all-to-all traces and hard bounds. Timing is referenced to presynaptic arrival. Pairing prescribes both spike trains; probes freeze learning and compute the target response. Weight is a dimensionless model efficacy, not anatomy, memory quality or a chemical concentration.

lif-model.title: Neuronal Dynamics §1.3: Integrate-and-fire models
lif-model.finding: Passive membrane leak, input integration, a threshold and reset provide a reduced description of spiking. Pulse input can be represented as a voltage jump.
lif-model.limit: No ion-channel waveform, spatial dendritic integration or receptor kinetics is calculated. doke parameters are pedagogical, not fitted to a human recording. Cell geometry, glow persistence and contact size are visual encodings.

stdp-limits.title: Triplets of spikes in a model of spike timing-dependent plasticity
stdp-limits.method: Model comparison with experimental plasticity protocols
stdp-limits.finding: Triplet interactions explain frequency and higher-order spike-pattern effects that basic pair-based rules cannot capture.
stdp-limits.limit: The first doke experiment deliberately uses a simpler pair rule. Its predictions should not be generalized to arbitrary activity patterns, all cell types or biological learning as a whole.

structure-dopamine.title: Dopamine — PubChem compound record
structure-dopamine.finding: Atom identities, bond orders and one 3D conformer provide the displayed ball-and-stick structure.
structure-dopamine.limit: One structure, not molecular dynamics. Hydrogen and protonation states follow the source record; L-glutamic acid is the conjugate acid of physiological glutamate. Display radii are illustrative.

structure-glutamate.title: L-glutamic acid — PubChem compound record
structure-glutamate.finding: Atom identities, bond orders and one 3D conformer provide the displayed ball-and-stick structure.
structure-glutamate.limit: One structure, not molecular dynamics. Hydrogen and protonation states follow the source record; L-glutamic acid is the conjugate acid of physiological glutamate. Display radii are illustrative.

structure-gaba.title: GABA — PubChem compound record
structure-gaba.finding: Atom identities, bond orders and one 3D conformer provide the displayed ball-and-stick structure.
structure-gaba.limit: One structure, not molecular dynamics. Hydrogen and protonation states follow the source record; L-glutamic acid is the conjugate acid of physiological glutamate. Display radii are illustrative.

motor.summary: On the frontal side of the central sulcus, the precentral gyrus includes primary motor cortex. It participates in control of voluntary movement.

prefrontal.summary: These frontal gyri participate in planning, working memory and cognitive control. Their contributions depend on the task and their interactions with other regions.

inferior-frontal.summary: Inferior frontal regions participate in language and control processes. A broad anatomical gyrus is not identical to a functional language area.

orbitofrontal.summary: Orbital frontal regions participate in evaluating outcomes and guiding decisions in context. Valuation is distributed across several interacting structures.

somatosensory.summary: The postcentral gyrus includes primary somatosensory cortex, which processes information about the body. The atlas does not resolve a particular finger representation.

parietal.summary: Superior parietal regions participate in spatial processing and coordination of sensory information with action.

inferior-parietal.summary: The angular and supramarginal gyri sit at an association-cortex crossroads. Their roles include integration across sensory and cognitive domains.

precuneus.summary: A medial parietal region involved in several internally directed and spatial processes. It participates in distributed networks rather than a single isolated function.

superior-temporal.summary: Superior temporal regions participate in auditory processing. This teaching group also includes adjacent temporal landmarks named in the atlas.

middle-temporal.summary: A temporal association region. The atlas defines its anatomical boundary; functional patterns can span it and neighboring cortex.

inferior-temporal.summary: Part of the broader ventral visual system involved in object representations. Information is distributed across overlapping response patterns.

fusiform.summary: The fusiform gyrus lies on the ventral temporal-occipital surface. It participates in visual recognition; the entire gyrus is not a dedicated “face center.”

auditory.summary: Heschl’s gyrus is an important auditory landmark on the superior temporal plane. It becomes easier to inspect when the surrounding cortex is hidden.

visual.summary: Occipital structures participate in visual processing. This grouped mesh contains several anatomical labels and does not delineate every visual area.

insula.summary: The insula lies within the lateral sulcus, beneath surrounding cortex. Its broad roles include integration of bodily and sensory information.

anterior-cingulate.summary: Anterior cingulate regions participate in control, motivation and affect-related processes. Activity here does not establish one specific emotion.

posterior-cingulate.summary: Posterior medial cortex participates in intrinsic functional networks. Its involvement changes with task and context.

parahippocampal.summary: These medial temporal gyri neighbor the hippocampus. This is an anatomical grouping, not a claim of a single memory pathway.

hippocampus.summary: The hippocampus participates in forming and organizing memories, in interaction with a wider medial temporal and cortical system.

amygdala.summary: An anatomically complex set of nuclei in the medial temporal lobe. It participates in learning and the relevance of stimuli, beyond any one emotion.

caudate.summary: A striatal structure with head, body and tail. In the music study, caudate responses were associated with anticipation of peak emotion.

putamen.summary: A striatal structure involved in basal ganglia circuits, including those concerned with action.

accumbens.summary: Part of the ventral striatum. The music study associated this region with peak pleasurable responses; this does not make it a universal pleasure meter.

pallidum.summary: The internal and external pallidal segments participate in basal ganglia circuits. This teaching mesh groups both segments.

thalamus.summary: A collection of nuclei that relay and regulate information in interactions with cortex and other structures. This mesh groups multiple atlas nuclei.

hypothalamus.summary: A small, diverse region involved in bodily regulation and neuroendocrine functions. Its nuclei have distinct roles that are not resolved by a single global activity value.

basal-forebrain.summary: An anatomical teaching group combining basal forebrain, septal and neighboring atlas labels. Individual cell populations and projections have different signaling roles.

substantia-nigra.summary: A midbrain structure participating in basal ganglia circuits. Dopaminergic neurons are associated with its pars compacta; the atlas mesh does not separate all cell types.

midbrain.summary: This teaching group combines midbrain tegmental and orienting structures. It is not a cell-specific dopamine source map.

cerebellum.summary: The cerebellum contributes to coordination and learning of movement, alongside broader cognitive roles. It interacts with systems outside the cerebellum.

pons.summary: The pons is part of the brainstem. This mesh combines atlas subdivisions and a connecting cerebellar peduncle for anatomical context.

medulla.summary: The medulla contains systems involved in autonomic regulation and pathways between brain and body. The displayed group includes adjacent labeled hindbrain tissue.

callosum.summary: The corpus callosum is a major white matter connection between the cerebral hemispheres. A bundle is not a single axon or a single signal.

white-matter.summary: White matter contains axonal pathways. Its dense internal atlas mesh is omitted from rendering to keep deeper structures visible.

olfactory.summary: This group contains the olfactory bulb, anterior olfactory nucleus and nearby olfactory cortical labels. Its boundaries come from the atlas ontology.

subthalamic.summary: A small nucleus participating in basal ganglia circuitry. Its role depends on its connections and activity patterns.

other-deep.summary: Context group: claustrum, habenular nuclei, pineal body and zona incerta. They are separate anatomical structures with different functions, grouped only for this overview.

activities.title: When music moves you
activities.intro: The moment before your favorite part. Then the part itself. Explore two phases of a studied musical experience.

chapters.title: Set the scene
chapters.text: The study used emotionally powerful music selected for the listeners. This story illustrates the findings; it does not measure your response to a song.

chapters.title: Anticipation
chapters.text: Bring the caudate into view. Anticipation and peak emotion were associated with different striatal responses in this study.

chapters.title: The peak
chapters.text: Now locate the nucleus accumbens. This chapter illustrates its association with the experience of peak emotion.

chapters.title: A chemical signal
chapters.text: Dopamine release, its synthesis, and receptor action are different processes. Open the synapse lesson to examine signaling at a smaller scale.

activities.title: The surprise in a reward
activities.intro: An expected outcome and a surprising one are not the same event for a learning system.

chapters.title: An unexpected outcome
chapters.text: A reward can produce a response when it was not predicted. The highlighted human structures provide schematic anatomical context.

chapters.title: Learn the cue
chapters.text: With learning, a reward-predicting cue can acquire a response. This is an explanatory sequence, not a fitted learning trajectory.

chapters.title: Expected or omitted?
chapters.text: Compare a predicted outcome with its omission. A negative prediction error is different from “no dopamine anywhere.”

chapters.title: A learning signal
chapters.text: The idea is a difference between prediction and outcome. It does not mean that every dopaminergic neuron carries the same signal.

activities.title: More than meets the eye
activities.intro: Recognition is a pattern across a system. Look beyond a single bright spot.

chapters.title: An anatomical starting point
chapters.text: Find occipital cortex and the ventral temporal surface. These are broad atlas landmarks for the visual system.

chapters.title: A distributed pattern
chapters.text: Ventral temporal response patterns can distinguish faces and objects. Several regions are highlighted to illustrate distribution.

chapters.title: Overlapping representations
chapters.text: Switch face and object conditions. The illustrative patterns overlap; the entire fusiform gyrus is not a dedicated face detector.

chapters.title: What was measured?
chapters.text: The study measured fMRI patterns. This does not specify individual spikes or task-evoked glutamate quantities.

activities.title: A small move. A whole system.
activities.intro: A simple movement offers a window onto coordinated brain function.

chapters.title: A defined task
chapters.text: Choose a hand for the teaching scenario. The atlas cannot resolve the exact neurons responsible for your movement.

chapters.title: Motor cortex
chapters.text: Inspect the precentral gyrus. Contralateral emphasis is an introductory simplification; both hemispheres can participate.

chapters.title: A wider system
chapters.text: Cerebellar and basal ganglia systems contribute to movement. These paths are schematic relationships, not reconstructed axon trajectories.

chapters.title: Sensation and action
chapters.text: Sensory information participates in ongoing movement. Region brightness represents authored emphasis, not a measured firing rate.

chemicals.name: Dopamine
chemicals.summary: Dopamine participates in learning, movement and other functions. Its effect depends on the pathway, receptor and state of the receiving cells.
chemicals.synthesis: Tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine. Synthesis is a biochemical process inside appropriate cells; a chosen activity does not specify its rate.
chemicals.release: Release occurs from dopaminergic terminals. The music lesson links to a study-specific inference about striatal release.
chemicals.receptors: Dopamine receptors are metabotropic: they influence intracellular signaling. This is distinct from a transmitter directly opening an ion channel.
chemicals.clearance: Transporters and metabolism help regulate the signal. The animation does not model calibrated dopamine kinetics.

chemicals.name: Glutamate
chemicals.summary: A major excitatory transmitter in the adult brain, acting through several ionotropic and metabotropic receptor types.
chemicals.synthesis: Neurons can form glutamate from metabolic precursors. Recycling between neurons and glia helps sustain signaling.
chemicals.release: Vesicles release glutamate at appropriate terminals. The lesson illustrates a representative chemical synapse.
chemicals.receptors: AMPA and NMDA are ionotropic receptor families; metabotropic glutamate receptors signal through G proteins. The synapse lesson uses an AMPA-like example.
chemicals.clearance: Transporters in neurons and glia remove glutamate from extracellular space. This is distinct from a synapse simply “turning off.”

chemicals.name: GABA
chemicals.summary: A major inhibitory transmitter in the mature brain. Effects depend on receptor type and ionic conditions, so inhibition is not a universal property in every context.
chemicals.synthesis: GABA can be synthesized from glutamate by glutamic acid decarboxylase in GABAergic neurons.
chemicals.release: GABAergic terminals release GABA. A whole-region highlight cannot identify the activity of all inhibitory cells.
chemicals.receptors: GABA-A receptors are ionotropic; GABA-B receptors are metabotropic. The neural circuit illustrates inhibitory population interactions, not receptor-specific kinetics.
chemicals.clearance: Transporters contribute to GABA uptake. Signaling and recycling occur alongside ongoing network activity.
